problems.title: Parking Lot System
problems.description: Build an in-memory parking lot with several floors. Bikes, cars, and trucks need different spot sizes. Issue a ticket on entry and charge for time on exit. Make it possible to add spot types and pricing rules without rewriting the whole parking flow.

must_have: Multiple floors, each with a typed list of ParkingSpot (SMALL/MEDIUM/LARGE).
Vehicle hierarchy: Bike → SMALL, Car → MEDIUM, Truck → LARGE.
park(Vehicle) issues a Ticket; unpark(ticketId) vacates the spot and computes price.
Availability display grouped by floor and spot type.
nice_to_have: Multiple gates with concurrent access (ReentrantLock or synchronized block).
EV charging spots (new SpotType + strategy extension).
clarifying_questions: Should one vehicle ever occupy more than one spot? (Assume NO for V1.)
Nearest-first or first-fit allocation — does it matter to you for V1?
Is pricing hourly only, or should PricingStrategy be injected from day one?
Do gates belong in the base design, or can I call park/unpark directly on ParkingLot?
Should duplicate vehicle (same plate number) prevent re-entry?

classes.name: ParkingLot
classes.responsibility:
Single orchestrator: own floors, strategies, and the active-ticket registry. Delegates allocation to ParkingStrategy and billing to PricingStrategy.

Does NOT calculate pricing or search spots directly.
classes.design_notes: Apply Singleton pattern if the problem implies one shared lot. Use ReentrantLock around spot assignment to prevent concurrent double-booking at multiple gates.

classes.name: Floor
classes.responsibility: Maintain an ordered list of ParkingSpot objects for one level. Does NOT contain business rules — it is a structural container.
classes.design_notes: Keep Floor dumb. Spot-finding logic belongs in ParkingStrategy, not here.

classes.name: ParkingSpot
classes.responsibility:
Represent one physical slot. Track type, occupancy, and current vehicle.

Expose occupy/vacate with minimal coupling to the lot.
methods: canFit(Vehicle v) : boolean  // optional if type-matching is in strategy
classes.design_notes: Do NOT put SpotType-to-VehicleType mapping here; it couples the spot to vehicle business rules. Keep it in the strategy.

classes.name: Vehicle
classes.responsibility: Abstract base carrying licensePlate and VehicleType. Subclasses (Bike, Car, Truck) exist to model the real world and allow future per-type overrides.
classes.design_notes: Java: abstract class Vehicle, then class Car extends Vehicle. Ruby: base class with attr_reader. Truck/Bike sub-classes each call super with fixed type.

classes.name: Ticket
classes.responsibility: Immutable receipt linking a vehicle, spot, and entry timestamp. Needed by PricingStrategy to compute billing.
classes.design_notes: Created inside park(); stored in ParkingLot.activeTickets. Removed on unpark.

classes.name: ParkingStrategy (interface)
classes.responsibility: Encapsulate the allocation algorithm. Allows swapping NearestFirst, SpreadEvenly, or any future strategy without changing ParkingLot.
classes.design_notes: NearestFirstParkingStrategy: iterate floors and spots in order, return first match by SpotType. Throws ParkingLotFullException if none found.

classes.name: PricingStrategy (interface)
classes.responsibility:
Encapsulate billing logic. HourlyPricingStrategy computes price from ticket entry time to now.

Swap in FlatRatePricingStrategy or SurgePricingStrategy without touching ParkingLot.
classes.design_notes: HourlyPricing: use Duration.between(entryTime, now()).toHours() × rate. For interview, you can hardcode rate=10.0 and note it is configurable.

relationships: ParkingLot 1..* Floor  (composition — floors die with lot)
ParkingLot depends on ParkingStrategy  (injected, not owned)
ParkingLot depends on PricingStrategy  (injected, not owned)
Ticket 1..1 ParkingSpot  (association — spot snapshot at entry)

design_patterns.name: Strategy
design_patterns.why:
Both allocation and pricing are volatile policies. Without Strategy, adding a new algorithm forces edits to ParkingLot (OCP violation).

With Strategy, you new NearestFirstParkingStrategy() and inject — zero changes to the orchestrator.
design_patterns.signal_phrase: I am separating allocation and pricing into strategies so the lot doesn't need to change when we add flat-rate weekends or EV-only spots.

design_patterns.name: Singleton
design_patterns.applied_to: ParkingLot instance (optional but common interview shorthand)
design_patterns.why:
A real parking lot is one physical entity; making the Java class a Singleton mirrors that reality and avoids accidental multi-instance ticket conflicts.

Always mention: in production I would use DI instead of static getInstance().
design_patterns.signal_phrase: I am using Singleton as an interview shorthand because there is physically one lot. In production I would inject ParkingLot through the DI framework.

design_patterns.name: Factory
design_patterns.why: VehicleFactory.create(type, plate) hides the constructor branching. Useful if the interviewer mentions a factory or you want to show knowledge of the pattern.
design_patterns.signal_phrase: I could add a VehicleFactory to centralise subclass construction, but for now new Car(plate) is readable enough.

design_patterns.name: Template Method (implicit)
design_patterns.why: Vehicle defines the shared contract (getType, getLicensePlate) and subclasses supply the fixed VehicleType. This is Template Method in miniature.
design_patterns.signal_phrase: Vehicle forces a consistent API — any new vehicle type just supplies its type constant and nothing else.

implementation_order: 1. Enums — VehicleType {BIKE, CAR, TRUCK}, SpotType {SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE}
3. Vehicle abstract class + Bike / Car / Truck subclasses
9. ParkingLot — park(), unpark(), displayAvailability() + optional Singleton
10. Demo driver: init floors → init lot → park bike/car/truck → display → unpark → reprice
key_phrases: I will keep persistence and payment integration out of scope and focus on an extensible in-memory core.
ParkingLot should orchestrate — it should not absorb allocation logic, pricing rules, or notification concerns.
If the interviewer adds EV charging spots later, that change is localised to a new SpotType enum value and a new allocation strategy — ParkingLot itself stays untouched.
The ReentrantLock around spot assignment prevents two concurrent gate threads from giving the same spot to two vehicles.
I am using Singleton as an interview shorthand; in production I would inject ParkingLot via a DI container.
gotchas: SOLID violation: Putting vehicle-to-spot mapping inside ParkingSpot or ParkingLot directly (SRP + OCP break). Put it in the strategy.
SOLID violation: God-class ParkingLot that calculates price, finds spots, manages exceptions AND sends notifications — extract each concern.
Bug: Forgetting to vacate() the ParkingSpot when unparking — spot stays occupied forever.
Bug: Not removing the ticket from activeTickets on unpark — ticket remains valid for a second free exit.
Edge case: Duplicate vehicle (same plate) already inside — check activeTickets by licensePlate before issuing new ticket.
Edge case: Invalid ticket ID on unpark — always throw InvalidTicketException, never silently ignore.
Design flaw: Hard-coding SpotType→VehicleType mapping as string comparisons instead of enum relationship.
Performance note: NearestFirst is O(floors × spots). Mention that a PriorityQueue of available spots per SpotType brings it to O(log n) — but O(n) is fine for the interview.
framework.extensibility_test:
Interviewer says: 'Add EV charging spots and priority handicapped parking.' Walk through: (1) Add EV and ACCESSIBLE to SpotType enum, (2) Add HANDICAPPED_VEHICLE to VehicleType, (3) Create AccessibleParkingStrategy that checks permit flag on Vehicle before assigning spot, (4) ParkingLot gets new strategy injected — zero change to its core logic.

This demonstrates OCP, Strategy, and DIP all in one answer.

clarify: State that persistent storage and payment gateway are out of scope upfront — this saves 5 minutes of dead-end discussion.
Ask: 'Is first-fit allocation acceptable for V1 or do you want nearest-spot optimisation?' — this positions you as thinking about trade-offs.
Call out duplicate vehicle and invalid ticket as the two primary error paths you will handle.
Decide on concurrency stance: 'I will mention thread-safety with a ReentrantLock and note it as a concern without over-engineering it.'
model: Start with the noun-from-requirements technique: ParkingLot, Floor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket are all nouns in the problem statement.
Model VehicleType and SpotType as enums immediately — never as raw strings.
ParkingLot OWNS its floors (composition). Strategy and PricingStrategy are INJECTED (dependency inversion).
Ticket is the join entity between a Vehicle and a ParkingSpot at a point in time — include entryTime for billing.
design: Introduce ParkingStrategy and PricingStrategy interfaces BEFORE writing any implementations. Explain WHY (OCP, DIP, replaceability).
Name your exceptions first: ParkingLotFullException and InvalidTicketException. Custom exceptions are a signal of maturity.
Explicitly say: 'ParkingLot is an orchestrator, not a pricing engine or a spot-finder. It delegates both concerns.'
Optional: mention Singleton with the caveat about DI in production.
implement: Code in this exact order: enums → exceptions → models (Vehicle hierarchy, ParkingSpot, Floor, Ticket) → interfaces (ParkingStrategy, PricingStrategy) → implementations → ParkingLot → Demo.
NearestFirstParkingStrategy: nested loop over floors then spots. mapVehicleToSpotType() is a private helper inside the strategy — keeps the mapping in one place.
In park(): lock → findSpot → spot.park(vehicle) → create Ticket → activeTickets.put → return Ticket.
In unpark(): get ticket → spot.vacate() → compute price → activeTickets.remove → return price.
review: Edge case: Duplicate vehicle on entry — check if plate exists in activeTickets values before assigning new spot.
Concurrency: 'At multi-gate scenarios, two threads could assign the same spot. My ReentrantLock ensures only one thread does spot assignment at a time.'
Extensibility answer: 'EV spots → add SpotType.EV, add EVParkingStrategy, inject it. Zero change to ParkingLot or Floor.'
Performance: 'NearestFirst is O(n) where n = total spots. For scale, I would maintain a PriorityQueue<ParkingSpot> per SpotType per floor, making allocation O(log n).'

checkpoints: Must-haves and out-of-scope are explicit before drawing any class.
Vehicle-to-SpotType mapping is type-safe (no string comparisons).
ParkingStrategy and PricingStrategy interfaces exist BEFORE their implementations.
ParkingLot only calls strategy.findSpot() and pricing.calculatePrice() — it does not contain those algorithms.
park() and unpark() both handle their primary error paths (full lot, invalid ticket).
Demo driver shows park → display → unpark → reprice as a runnable sequence.

interview.opening_prompt: Design a parking lot system that supports multi-floor parking, typed spots for bikes/cars/trucks, ticketing, and pricing. Before you name a single class, tell me what you are leaving out of scope and what the two most important error conditions are.
evaluation_rubric: Requirement scoping: Does the candidate explicitly bucket must-haves and out-of-scope before touching any design?
Entity modeling clarity: Are Vehicle, ParkingSpot, Floor, and Ticket named with the right ownership boundaries?
Strategy abstractions: Are ParkingStrategy and PricingStrategy introduced as interfaces before any implementation?
FIT rules: Is VehicleType→SpotType mapping type-safe and located in the strategy, not scattered?
Error paths: Are ParkingLotFullException and InvalidTicketException explicit custom exceptions?
Extensibility proof: Can the candidate add EV spots without touching ParkingLot?
probing_questions: Why did you choose to put the vehicle-to-spot mapping inside the strategy instead of inside ParkingSpot?
What happens if two gate attendants try to park vehicles at the exact same moment?
How would you change this design if the pricing needed to vary by time of day?
Walk me through the exact sequence of method calls from a car arriving at the gate to the ticket being issued.
If I told you we now need 50% priority spots for electric vehicles — what is the minimum code change?

sections.heading: Why Strategy Pattern is Non-Negotiable Here
sections.content:
Without Strategy, every new pricing policy (flat-rate, surge, member discount) requires editing ParkingLot.unpark() — an OCP violation.

Without Strategy for allocation, adding EV-only spots requires adding an if-else inside park() — again an OCP violation. Strategy = the interviewer's first check for extensibility reasoning.

sections.heading: The Lock Dilemma
sections.content:
Two threads (two gates) executing findSpot() concurrently will both see the same free spot. Thread A calls spot.park(vehicle1) first, then Thread B also calls spot.park(vehicle2) — one car has no spot.

Fix: ReentrantLock.lock() before findSpot, unlock in finally. Mention ConcurrentHashMap for activeTickets (safe reads at all times).

Say: 'I am aware this is a simplification; at scale I would use a distributed lock or a seat-reservation pattern with optimistic locking.'

sections.heading: The Fit Rule Placement Problem
sections.content:
Where does Vehicle→SpotType mapping live? BAD: Inside ParkingSpot (spot knows too much about vehicles).

BAD: Inside ParkingLot (God class). CORRECT: Inside NearestFirstParkingStrategy, in a private mapVehicleToSpotType() helper.

This is the Strategy owning its own logic. When you add EVParkingStrategy, it can have a completely different (or override-based) mapping.

sections.heading: Ticket as the Join Entity
sections.content:
Ticket is classically a join table in relational design — the bridge between Vehicle (the owner) and ParkingSpot (the resource) at a specific instant.

It carries entryTime which is the key piece of data needed by PricingStrategy. Without Ticket, unpark() has no way to know when the vehicle entered.

sections.heading: Singleton — Use Deliberately, Justify It
sections.content:
Singleton is fine for this problem IF you justify it: 'A real parking lot is one physical entity; I am reflecting that in code.' The red flag is using Singleton everywhere without justification.

Always add the caveat: 'In production I would inject this through a DI container instead of getInstance().'

common_interview_dialogues.interviewer: Can you walk me through how a Car parks?
common_interview_dialogues.ideal_response: Sure. The caller creates new Car('KA-01') and calls parkingLot.park(car). Inside park(), we lock first to prevent concurrent spot conflicts. Then strategy.findSpot(CAR, floors) is called — NearestFirstStrategy maps CAR to MEDIUM spot type and iterates floors floor by floor, spot by spot, returning the first free MEDIUM spot. spot.park(car) marks it occupied. We generate a ticket ID, create Ticket(id, car, spot), store it in activeTickets, unlock, and return the Ticket. The caller keeps the Ticket for exit.

common_interview_dialogues.interviewer: What if two cars try to park at the same time?
common_interview_dialogues.ideal_response: That is the concurrent gate problem. Without a lock, both threads could see Spot 101 as free, both call spot.park(), and one car ends up without a spot. My ReentrantLock around findSpot + park ensures only one thread does this atomic operation at a time. In a distributed environment I would use a distributed lock (Redis SETNX) or an optimistic locking strategy with a version field on ParkingSpot.

common_interview_dialogues.interviewer: How do you add EV charging spots?
common_interview_dialogues.ideal_response: Three localized changes: (1) Add EV to SpotType enum, (2) Add new EVParkingStrategy that maps EVVehicle→SpotType.EV with an additional is-charger-available check, (3) Inject the new strategy into ParkingLot. ParkingLot code, Floor code, ParkingSpot code — none of them change. This is OCP in practice.

complexity_analysis.park_time: O(F × S) where F = floors, S = spots per floor — NearestFirst linear scan. O(log n) with PriorityQueue<ParkingSpot> per type.
complexity_analysis.space: O(F × S) for spot storage + O(T) for active tickets where T = parked vehicles.

deep_dive.java_full_reference: The complete annotated Java implementation is in swe-mastery-journal/LLD/code/01-parking-lot/java_demo/ParkingLotDemo.java — use it as the gold-standard reference for interview implementation order and comment quality.
deep_dive.ruby_reference: The Ruby implementation is in swe-mastery-journal/LLD/code/01-parking-lot/ruby/parking_lot.rb — shows how Strategy and Singleton translate to Ruby duck-typing and the Singleton module.

problems.title: Snake and Ladder
problems.description: Build a turn-based board game. Players roll a die and move across the board. Snakes move them back; ladders move them forward. Define the order of turns and the rule for winning.

must_have: Board of size N x N (typically 10x10 = 100 cells)
Player must land exactly on 100 to win (or overshoot handling)
Game ends when a player reaches the last cell
nice_to_have: Crooked dice (always returns even number — for testing)
clarifying_questions: What happens if a player is at 98 and rolls a 5? Do they stay at 98, bounce back? (Assume they stay in place for V1)
Can multiple players be on the same cell?
Can a ladder lead to a snake's head?

classes.name: Game
classes.responsibility: Orchestrates the game loop, maintains player queue, and checks for game ends. Does not contain board physics.
classes.design_notes: Maintains the state machine of the game and the turn loop. Belongs at the top level.

classes.name: Board
classes.responsibility: Holds jump mappings (snakes and ladders) and validates moves. Does NOT hold players.
classes.design_notes: Use a jumpMap (hashmap) instead of individual Snake/Ladder classes if they only serve as jumps. Or model Snake/Ladder entities composed in the map. Keeps physics separate from players.

classes.name: Player
classes.responsibility: Maintains player state like name and current position.
classes.design_notes: A dumb entity. Does not roll the dice or move itself by reaching into the board; Game coordinates this.

classes.name: Dice (Interface)
classes.design_notes: Interface allows NormalDice and CrookedDice (for testing/variation).

relationships: Board 1..* Jump (Snake/Ladder entities or simple Map)

design_patterns.name: Strategy
design_patterns.why: Allows swapping out NormalDice with a CrookedDice (always throws even numbers) for easy unit testing.
design_patterns.signal_phrase: I'll make Dice an interface to implement the Strategy pattern. This allows us to inject a deterministic CrookedDice later for testing without mocking.

implementation_order: 3. Board class (setup jump map, move logic)
key_phrases: I'm keeping Players out of the Board to satisfy Single Responsibility. The Board handles physics, the Player handles identity, and the Game orchestrates.
Instead of treating Snake and Ladder as separate domain classes with logic, I'll model them as a simple Map of start -> end positions to keep O(1) jump lookups.
I'll use a Queue for players to handle turn logic simply by polling and appending until a win is detected.
gotchas: SOLID violation: Adding `rollDice()` inside `Player`. Player shouldn't hold the random generator logic.
Bug: Unbounded jumps — what if a ladder leads to a snake? Make sure jumps are computed correctly without infinite loops.
Edge case: Dice rolls 5 when player is at 98 (needs 2 to win). Ensure logic clearly skips or handles overshoot safely.
framework.extensibility_test:
Interviewer says: 'We want multiple dice'. Candidate: 'Since Dice is an interface, I can create a MultipleDiceStrategy that rolls N times and sums the result.

Game doesn't change.'

clarify: Ask what happens on overshoot (e.g., at 98, rolls 4).
Ask if multiple players can occupy the same spot.
model: Jump mappings can just be a HashMap<Integer, Integer> where key=start, value=end. No need for complex objects.
Use a Queue for round-robin turn management.
design: Make Dice an interface. It shows you think about testability.
Separate Board limits from turn orchestration.
implement: Start with small entities: Player, Dice.
In Game play(), use a while loop until isOver.
review: Mention how the Dice interface makes unit testing deterministic.

checkpoints: Clarified target exact win vs overshoot rules.
Game loop uses a Queue for robust turns.

interview.opening_prompt: Design the classic Snake and Ladder game. Focus on the core mechanics and game loop. What are the key entities and how do they interact?
evaluation_rubric: Does the candidate separate game orchestration from board topography?
Are jumps modeled efficiently (O(1) lookup vs O(N) iteration)?
Is the turn mechanism simple (like a Queue) instead of messy index tracking?
Can they articulate how to test it without random flaky tests?
probing_questions: How would you handle a scenario where a ladder takes you directly into a snake's mouth?
If I asked you to write a unit test for a player winning, how does your Dice design enforce a predictable test?

sections.heading: Why Jump Maps?
sections.content:
Beginners often create `Snake` and `Ladder` classes. While purely OOP, traversing a List<Snake> to check if a cell has a snake is O(S).

A simple `Map<Integer, Integer>` where key is start cell (head of snake or bottom of ladder) and value is end cell, handles both instantly in O(1) and simplifies `Board`.

sections.heading: Queue for Turns
sections.content:
Managing turns with `currentPlayerIndex = (currentPlayerIndex + 1) % players.size()` works but is brittle if players are removed.

Using a `Queue` where you `poll()` the current player and `offer()` them back at the end of their turn is much cleaner.

sections.heading: Testability with Dice Strategy
sections.content:
Testing games of chance is notoriously hard. If `Dice` is hardcoded to `Math.random()`, you can't assert a win sequence reliably.

Extracting `Dice` interface allows injecting a `CrookedDice` or `MockDice` that returns exact sequences [4, 6, 2] in tests.

common_interview_dialogues.interviewer: Where shouldn't the roll dice logic go?
common_interview_dialogues.ideal_response: It shouldn't be inside the `Player` class. The player is a state holder. Pushing action dependencies like `Dice` into `Player` violates SRP. The `Game` orchestrator should roll the dice and then tell the player where they landed based on the board.

complexity_analysis.move_time: O(1) to map dice roll and jump lookup.
complexity_analysis.space: O(S + L + P) for Snakes, Ladders, and Players.

problems.title: Tic Tac Toe
problems.description: Build a game for two players. Accept a move only in an empty cell and on the correct turn. Check for a winner or draw after each move. Keep the rules clear enough to support a different board size if required.

must_have: Two players with distinct symbols (X and O)
Win detection — row, column, or diagonal filled by same symbol
Draw detection — board full with no winner
Input validation — cell must be empty and within bounds
nice_to_have: N x N board with configurable win condition
Multiple game rounds with score tracking
clarifying_questions: Is the board strictly 3x3 or should it scale to NxN?
Is the win condition always filling the entire row/col, or K-in-a-row?
Do we need bot players, or just human vs human?

classes.name: Game
classes.responsibility: Orchestrates players and board, manages turn state, and checks win status.
classes.design_notes: Similar to Snake and Ladder, the Game loop is the orchestrator.

classes.name: Board
classes.responsibility: Holds grid state, sets symbols, and validates bounds.
classes.design_notes: Board manages spatial data but arguably win detection can live here or in an external RuleEngine.

classes.name: Player
classes.responsibility: Represents a participant, holding their symbol and name.
classes.design_notes: If bot support is required, Player acts as context for a PlayerStrategy.

classes.name: PlayerStrategy (Interface)
classes.design_notes: HumanStrategy reads from console; BotStrategy computes.

design_patterns.name: Strategy
design_patterns.why: Allows treating human input and bot algorithms uniformly in the game loop.
design_patterns.signal_phrase: I will extract move generation into a PlayerStrategy interface so the Game doesn't need 'if bot then... else...' logic.

implementation_order: 2. Board: setup grid, print method, boundary checks
3. PlayerStrategy & Player: Move data object, Human entry
key_phrases: Checking the whole board on every turn is O(N^2). I will implement a localized win check that only scans the row, column, and diagonals anchored to the last placed symbol, bringing it to O(N).
By associating the move selection with a Strategy, adding a Minimax bot later requires zero changes to the Game class.
gotchas: Performance detail: Standard check is O(N^2). Optimized check is O(N).
Bug: Not checking if a cell is already occupied before placing.
SOLID Violation: Putting `Scanner` or `System.in` directly inside `Player` or `Game`.
framework.extensibility_test:
Interviewer says: 'Add a computer player.' Candidate: 'I implement a BotStrategy (perhaps picking random empty cells or Minimax). I initialize a Player with BotStrategy.

Game loop just calls `player.makeMove(board)` — it works automatically.'

clarify: Ask if the board is strictly 3x3 or scalable.
model: Make Symbol an Enum, not strings/chars.
design: Keep I/O (Scanner) out of Game core. Abstract it via HumanStrategy.
review: Walk through the last-move win optimization.

checkpoints: Win Check is O(N), not O(N^2).
Move fetching is abstracted into a Strategy.

interview.opening_prompt: Let's design Tic Tac Toe. Before jumping into code, tell me how you will represent players to easily support computer opponents in the future, and how you will check for a winner efficiently.
evaluation_rubric: Strategy Pattern: Is move selection cleanly separated from player data?
Optimized validation: Is win detection O(N) relying on the last placed piece?
Extensibility: Does Game rely on hardcoded I/O?
probing_questions: Scanning the whole board takes O(N^2) time. How can you verify a win after a move in O(N) time?
What if we want an online matchmaking system later where moves come from an HTTP hook? How will this design adapt?

sections.heading: Optimizing Win Detection
sections.content:
A naive win check scans the entire board. But a win can only happen if the *last placed symbol* completes a line.

By passing `lastRow` and `lastCol` to `checkWin`, we only check `board[lastRow][...]`, `board[...][lastCol]`, and the two diagonals if the piece is on them. This reduces validation from O(N^2) to O(N).

sections.heading: Strategy for Moves
sections.content:
Using a `PlayerStrategy` for move fetching allows us to completely decouple the game rules from the I/O. `HumanStrategy` reads from standard input.

`BotStrategy` runs minimax. `NetworkStrategy` waits for JSON socket data.

The `Game` loop remains `player.makeMove()`.

common_interview_dialogues.interviewer: Can you do win detection in O(1)?
common_interview_dialogues.ideal_response: Yes, by maintaining running arrays. We keep a `rowCount[N]`, `colCount[N]`, `diag`, and `antiDiag`. When Player X moves at (r,c), we do `rowCount[r]++`. If any count reaches N, Player X wins. For Player O, we decrement. This makes win checks O(1) space O(N).

complexity_analysis.win_check: O(N) normal, O(1) with running row/col sums.

problems.title: Elevator System
problems.description: Manage several elevators and their requests. Choose which elevator should handle a call. Track its floor, direction, and pending stops. Keep the choice of scheduling rule separate from moving an elevator.

problems.title: Splitwise
problems.description: Track shared expenses and what each person owes. Support equal, exact, and percentage splits as required. Check that shares add up to the expense. Keep balances and settlements consistent.

problems.title: Movie Ticket Booking System
problems.description: Build a movie ticket booking flow. Users find a show, choose seats, and try to reserve them. Two users must not receive the same seat. Define what happens when a reservation expires or payment fails.

problems.title: Logging Framework
problems.description: Send log messages to the right destinations. Support log levels and different output formats. Allow a new destination or formatter without changing every caller. Decide how handlers pass a message along.

problems.title: LRU Cache
problems.description: Build a cache with a fixed capacity. Reads and updates should take O(1) time. When the cache is full, remove the least recently used entry. Keep the lookup map and usage order in sync.

problems.title: Vending Machine
problems.description: Build a machine that accepts coins and dispenses a selected product. Track stock, the current payment, and the machine’s state. Return change or reject an invalid action. Define what happens when a product is sold out.

problems.title: Ride Sharing System
problems.description: Match a rider’s request with an available driver. Track the trip from request to completion. Calculate the fare using a replaceable pricing rule. Reject actions that do not fit the current trip state.

problems.title: Rate Limiter
problems.description: Limit how many requests a user may make. Start with a token bucket and define how time refills it. Handle requests arriving at the same time. Keep the algorithm replaceable if the requirements change.

problems.title: Task Scheduler
problems.description: Schedule work for a later time. Support one-time and repeated tasks, priorities, and dependencies as required. Allow cancellation with clear rules. Decide who owns task state and how the next ready task is selected.
